speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: DEATH OF DOCTOR WILLIAM SPANKIE . TRIBUTES BY PRIME MINISTER, LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION AND MR. SPEAKMAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my sad and melancholy duty to inform the house that for the second time this session one of our members has been touched by the hand of death. Doctor William Spankie, the member for Fron-tenac-Addington, passed to his reward yesterday. He was a mueh-beloved member of this chamber. I think all who knew him held him in affectionate regard and esteem. He lived the greater part of his life in the community in which he was born, and he was family physician to practically three generations. Just what that meant people in these days have little opportunity of understanding, for the old fashioned physician, shall I say, with the changes that have led to greater complexity in our civilization has passed from the scene. That one who was a family physician for two or three generations would be greatly beloved goes without saying. His genial manner, wide knowledge of human nature, and his professional attainments, which had been recognized alike by the medical council of his province and of the dominion, made him a very popular figure in the community in which he lived. He took a deep and abiding interest in the public welfare. He was inspector of schools for many years, was greatly interested in educational matters in his province, and kept abreast of the great changes that have taken place in the medical profession, for as I say, he was plosely identified with the council of physicians and surgeons not only in Ontario but in the dominion as well.
His life was an arduous one, especially in the earlier days, when the work of his profession kept him moving from place to place on Wolfe Mand. He was accustomed to hardships and difficulties. That greatly endeared him to those whom he served. His popularity was such that when a vacancy occurred for the county in which he lived he was elected by acclamation and subsequently returned to this house.
He had attained the ripe age of seventy-four, being in his seventy-fifth year. He had given hostages to fortune, for three of his sons reside in the province in which I live, and two of them are members of the profession of Which he was an ornament. I am sure that to the survivors of his family, his Children, you, Mr. Speaker, will convey the sympathy of this house, for to the members of this chamber Doctor Spankie had endeared

Death of Doctor Spankie
himself by the kindliness of his nature and his genial personality. We shall miss him greatly. It is one more reminder to us of the uncertainty of life.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: DEATH OF DOCTOR WILLIAM SPANKIE . TRIBUTES BY PRIME MINISTER, LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION AND MR. SPEAKMAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tribute which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has just paid to ithe memory of the late member for Frontenac-Addington is not only worthy and merited but will be appreciated as well as approved by hon. members of all parties in this house. While it is true that Doctor Spankie owing to the recent date at which he was first elected and to his advanced years was a member of parliament for but a short time; while it is also true that largely because of an infirmity of hearing he participated but little in the debates of this house there could be no clearer evidence of the fineness of his personality and character than the fact that notwithstanding these handicaps he was able to impress both so greatly upon others. It should be recognized that after all, his years in parliament were but the crowning recognition of a long life of useful service to his fellowmen and to the country.
Doctor Spankie was a man who, above everything else, appeared to find his greatest joy in doing good, and in the service to others. The theatre of his public actions may have been circumscribed but there was inherent in the actions themselves the greatness which belongs to a reverence for the highest virtues. The choice of his profession indicated his sympathy with human suffering, and his desire to do what he could, in the course of his life, to aid in its alleviation. The Prime Minister has made reference to Doctor Spankie's interest in educational matters. The fact that he devoted so much time in the community in which he lived to the offices of school trustee and school inspector showed his desire to widen, by the surest method possible, the opportunities of the oncoming generation. The value which he attached to learning was also evidenced not only by his own university attainments, but by the fact that all four of his sons were given to the learned professions, two of them to the profession of medicine, and the other two to the profession of law. By his lifelong participation in municipal affairs as well as in dominion politics, he disclosed his belief in the importance of government in human affairs, and in the obligation resting upon those best qualified in their communities actively to share in public life. All were expressions of the many-sidedness of his
nature, which found itheir unity in the desire of service for others.
The Prime Minister has referred to Doctor Spankie as belonging to that class of family physician which is rapidly disappearing, and of whom too little is known even in our rural communities to-day, the general practitioner who in former years played such an important part in the life of the community in which he lived. I am sure no one familiar with modern literature could read the accounts that to-day are being given of Doctor Spankie's services to his community, his visits in mid-winter to outlying districts, driving himself his faithful horse, incurring all kinds of personal risks to serve some human need, without recalling that immortal chapter in Ian Maclaren's " Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush," entitled " The Doctor of the Old School." In a Canadian environment, not wholly dissimilar, he resembled in many particulars Doctor McLure of the Scottish glen. I thought I would find something there which would be appropriate to say in memory of him who is gone. I have a passage here which I think, perhaps is appropriate in its application to him, but is, I believe, even more appropriate to those of us who remain. It is a paragraph with which Maclaren concludes his account of the doctor's last journey:
After which the minister prayed, that we might have grace to live as this man had done from youth to age, not for himself, but for others, and that we might be followed to our grave by somewhat of "that love wherewith we mourn this day Thy servant departed."
On behalf of other members of the opposition and for myself personally I express to the Prime Minister and hon. gentlemen opposite our very sincere sympathy in the loss they have sustained, of so loyal and devoted a colleague; and I join with my right hon. friend in extending our deepest sympathies to those who by his death have been so greatly bereaved.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members in this corner of the house may I associate myself with the right lion. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in expressing our appreciation of the life and our regret at the death of our late colleague Doctor Spankie. Perhaps there is no gathering of men in which integrity of character and kindliness of disposition make themselves more effectually felt, seen and known than in this chamber. Both these qualities were possessed by Doctor Spankie. Because of that fact, and because at all times and to all
Marketing Act

men,, regardless of party, Doctor Spankie proved himself a friend, we join in regretting his passing and in expressing our condolences to those of his family who are left to mourn him.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, May 21, consideration in committee of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade; and to make further provisions in connection therewith-Mr. Weir (Melfort)-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 12, subsection (1)-Power to restrict importation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
During the interval since this bill was under discussion last we have drafted another clause which I think may meet some of the objections which were offered to section 12 when the bill was under discussion a few days ago. I will read the proposed new section, and submit it to hon. gentlemen for their consideration:
The governor in council may, by order or regulation, notice whereof shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette,-	_
(a)	regulate or restrict the importation into
Canada of any natural product which enters Canada in competition with a regulated product;	.
(b)	regulate or restrict the exportation from Canada of any natural product;
(c)	provide for the licensing of persons by whom any such natural product may be imported or exported;
(d)	prescribe the forms of such licences and the terms and conditions upon which the same may be issued, renewed, suspended or revoked by the governor in council.
Under this proposal it will be noted that the issuing and rescission of licenses will be placed under the jurisdiction of the governor in council and not under the minister, as was provided in the section as originally drafted. I am sending a copy to my right hon. friend. I believe the language in the amendment meets with some and perhaps all of the objections urged by him on former occasions.

speechtext: I think that every day in every way this bill is getting a little better, and we are encouraged not to persevere too much but, at all! events, to keep going, in order to make it even better. It is not much better, by this last amendment though, -not much, but just a little. I wonder if there could not be some explicit reservations. We know that the world is chock full of trade restrictions of all kinds, and this is one more added to a number which is already too great. This is a case of restricting trade first by prohibition, and then by restricting importation. Surely the government could at least tell us what this is for. What are they trying to do? Are they trying to blockade the trade of the country just a little more, or is some more useful purpose to be served? I can imagine a useful purpose which could be served. Low grade commodities, poor, bum live stock that we do not want in Canada could be kept out, and any provision with that in view would be a proper one. Then, there are some breeds of lard hogs which are not desirable. But to have an indefinite and indiscriminate restriction by a local board, the status of which we do not yet understand, is not surely right. We have done a great deal of gagging at some of the objectionable provisions of this bill, and I must say that this is one of the worst sections we have to yet swallow, or amend- for me, all events. Yet I can see sufficient good in it, if it is defined, to view it with some favour. But to make the provision without any reservation other than that now stated by the minister, one which makes it only infinitesimally better, does not seem to improve the major objection. I wonder if the minister could not help us out, and tell us what it is for. Personally, I believe it is to deal with some problems such as the butter question with which we were faced last year. We remember the importations of butter which were put into bond at Halifax and Vancouver, and held at those points until the market could absorb them. That would not be a bad reason for the change. But instead of leaving it as wide open as a barn door I suggest there should be some specifications which would make it at least more understandable and more commendable. Would the minister come to my relief in that regard?

As I read it,
apparently the amendment eliminates one objectionable clause. I should like to know if I am right in my assumption. The clause to which I am referring formerly read:
The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette,-
(c) impose penalties for breach of any such order or regulation or of any licence issued thereunder, and, generally, make such provision or authorize the doing of such acts or things as may in his discretion be deemed necessary or expedient for giving full effect to any orders, regulations or licences made or issued hereunder.

speechtext:
Yes. The section as it now stands means that the governor in council is to have the power to restrict the importations into the country and to restrict the exportations from the country of any regulated commodity the governor in council may wish to have so restricted. I say "any commodity" because another clause gives to the governor in council power to make any commodity coming within the definition of natural product, a regulated commodity, and this clause gives to the governor in council the power to require a licence with respect to the importation of or exportation of any regulated commodity.
The first exception I wish to take to this section is that it treats both exports and imports in the same way. Hon. gentlemen opposite have given certain reasons why some commodities should not be permitted to come into the country at certain times. They have not thus far given any reasons why commodities should not be exported from Canada, other than to oblige those nations which may have prohibitory tariffs or quotas against us, and to help to meet those prohibitions. It seems to me that is a mistaken attitude to take. People who are producing commodities know better than any other people where opportunities for their sale may lie, and what prohibitions they are likely to encounter. I think they might well be left to look after themselves in that regard, and should not be shouldered with the additional liability of having the government prohibit their exports. Such liability would be in addition to the prohibitions against the admission of their exports which might be made by certain countries. In the second place, this measure does not follow the British act in its essential provisions. The British act permits certain restrictions on the importations of regulated commodities, but it has nothing whatever to say of restricting exports. So far as I have been able to read both British acts dealing with marketing it would seem that they allow the producers and shippers and others concerned with the export of commodities the freest latitude.

speechtext:
And I do not see why we in this country need to begin to restrict exports. That brings us, it seems to me, to the fundamental criticism of this measure. It aims not at regulating trade but strikes at the very heart of the primary industries of this country, namely, the production that comes from the primary and basic industries. This country is dependent on its basic industries above all else, and the greatest freedom should be allowed in the production and distribution of our natural products. But this bill goes the length of seeking to limit the production of natural products by a regulation which will be carried out through ths instrumentality of licensing. Licensing simply means that producers will have to comply with whatever the governor in council wishes to lay down as conditions upon which exportation can take place. That I think is a very serious departure in the whole business of legislation respecting the trade of this country, and should not be countenanced because it may lead anywhere.
I come back to what I said a day or two ago, that I believe this desire to limit production and trade through the instrumentality of licensing exporters and importers is part of a broader plan which aims, and in the future will be seen to aim, at the regulation of trade within channels within the British Empire at the expense of world trade. The Minister of Agriculture said that I had a vivid imagination when I made the statement that the government might wish to restrict trade in a manner which would cause it to flow in chan-

nets within the British Empire, even if such were at the expense of world trade. But I find that exactly that kind of policy is being set forth in different parts of the British Empire aS the policy which certain governments should adopt.
I have in my hand a dispatch from London dated May 17, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 18 of this year, entitled, "Twofold policy now announced by Chamberlain. New world trade policy to which British government adheres outlined by Chancellor of Exchequer.1' The dispatch reads:
London, May 17.-The new world trading policy to which Premier MacDonald's government now adheres has just been officially announced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain.
A little further on:
The British cabinet has decided to develop a twofold policy in future of expanding the home market and developing inter-imperial agreements based on those of the Ottawa conference.
A little further on:
Our main preoccupation will be domestic trade expansion and extension of the Ottawa pacts to the utmost. With such an object in view the British government intends to initiate a series of consultations with overseas premiers.
A little further on:
Since the great slump began there has been a cessation of all foreign lending but lately representations have been made to the treasury to lift its ban on such loans. It is unlikely in view of the government's announced trade policy this will now be done.
Meanwhile the dominions will benefit. They will have full access to the London financial market.
In other words, there is distinctly set forth by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain an imperial trade policy and an imperial financial policy, each of which seeks to regulate both trade and finance within the British Empire I shall not be surprised if, when we come'to consider further the banking legislation in this house we will get still further evidence of the fact that it too is being fashioned by the government to accord with imperial policies of trade and finance.
In order that there may be no mistake about such a policy not being confined to Britain alone, let me make mention of a speech which hon. members no doubt either heard at the time or have since read which was recently made by the Prime Minister of Canada, in which he too dealt with the trading policy of his own administration. He defined it as a trading policy sealing empire unity. I have in my hand the account of the address

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
to which I refer, as it appears in the Ottawa Citizen of May 24. It was made by the Prime Minister on May 23 of this year when the Prime Minister was responding to the toast of Canada at the Royal Empire Society's annual banquet at Montreal on the night of the twenty-third instant. The dispatch has the following:
Speaking of the loyalty of empire peoples to the crown and the ties that bind the family of nations within the commonwealth, Mr. Bennett urged the necessity of evolving a common foreign trade policy which would seal and perpetuate the unity.
At that same gathering addresses were delivered by the trade commissioners from Australia, South Africa, New Zealand, the British West Indies and Bermuda. I have not any objection at all to the government having as its policy in matters of trade, an empire trade policy, but what I do take exception to is their lack of frankness and candour in not coming forward and saying that such is exactly what they have in mind. Instead of doing that they place on the statute books an act, under the guise of a measure to regulate marketing, which in reality so long as it contains the sections that we are discussing at the moment may be used, and I believe is intended to be used, to restrict exportation from this country of natural products where it may serve this imperial trade policy so to do, and equally to restrict imports into this country where it may serve this imperial trade policy so to do.
For my part I believe that what is best for Canada in the matter of trade is a world policy. I believe that as we build up our trade with all the nations of the world so will we build up a stronger Canada, and to that extent a stronger empire in virtue of Canada being a constituent element thereof.
There is another exception Mr. Chairman,
I wish to take to this section, and to it I wish to take very strong exception. It is that here again is a move to deprive individuals of their rights and their liberties at the instance of an arbitrary tribunal, and without permitting the redress which the courts of the land should be in a position to afford. That kind of thing has become so common in this country that it has already been commented upon by members of the judiciary, who are in an exceptional position to judge of infringements of the rights and the liberties of the individual. I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite say that if proceedings are to be begun under the provisions of the law which impose fines and penalties they will have to be taken in a court of the land where, those affected
will have all the protection which the law affords, and where they will not be deprived of their rights and liberties without due process of law. This section, however, says nothing whatever about any right of appeal to courts, only that the governor in council may determine who may import and who may export, and that he may do so by issuing licences, also that the governor in council is to determine under what conditions the licences are to be granted. I say that the moment a man is unable to secure a licence to import or a licence to export that very moment he is deprived of some of his rights and liberties, and according to this section if deprived he has no redress in the courts of the land because it is the governor in council who alone provides for the licensing and who alone determines what natural products may be imported or exported, and prescribes the forms of such licences and the terms and conditions upon which they may be given and revoked.
I referred last week to the important work by Lord Hewart the Chief Justice of Great Britain entitled The New Despotism, which takes exception ito this depriving of individuals of their rights and privileges and liberties by arbitrary action on the part of boards and councils, whether they be the governor in council or some other general or local boards, without the safeguarding of those rights and liberties by the kind of protection which the courts have been created to afford. I desire to quote now from a chief justice of our own country. I have in my hand a copy of a very notable address which was delivered by the Chief Justice of Ontario, the Right Hon. Sir William Mulock, a short time ago, at a dinner which was given in his honour by the Bar of the province of Ontario. Sir William Mulock has had exceptionally wide experience in the matter of legislation, and I do not think he can be accused of being other than a true friend of the farmers of this country. In this parliament he was always a champion of their rights. For twenty-three years the Right Honourable Sir William Mulock was a member of this House of Commons; for nine of those years he was a minister of the crown; for twenty-nine years he has been a judge of the High Court, during which time he has been Chief Justice of Ontario for eleven years. I submit that anything said by the Right Honourable Sir William Mulock with respect to legislation and its effects is deserving of very careful consideration by the Parliament of Canada. I quote from Sir William's Speech as reported in the Canadian Bar

Review of January, 1934. At page 38, he is reported as follows:
I desire to bring to your attention a subject of the greatest importance, one which concerns the liberties, the rights, the happiness of every citizen in Canada, and the welfare of Canada itself.	.	.	- ,,I refer to the ever-increasing practice or tne parliament of Canada and of our provincial legislatures of depriving our people of the protection	of	the	law and of	the courts,	byvesting in	autocratic bodies	the power	toarbitrarily deal with matters affecting our liberties and other rights without the intervention of any court.	.I wish it clearly understood that the views to which	I	am	giving expression have	noreference to the actions of any one political party, but are intended solely as an abstract criticism of	the	practice of	legislatures	inshutting the doors of the duly constituted courts of justice against any citizen, rich or poor, high or low, whatever be his position in the community, and leaving the decision of his legal rights at the mercy of any non-judicial body, often ignorant of the law, bound by no no iaw, free to disregard the evidence and the law, and practically at its own will, to dispose finally of his rights.	. .
Most people in Canada are of opinion that everywhere throughout the land the rule of law prevails and is sovereign guardian of their rights. It is not so.
For long years legislatures have encroached upon many of the people's most sacred rights, deprived them of the protection of the courts of justice, and conferred upon commissions, public officers and other irresponsible bodies the power of arbitrarily determining the people's rights.	.	J.	.
To this situation all political parties have contributed; and the fact that the people generally have acquiesced in such legislation indicates an alarming indifference of the people themselves to the public safety.
I think I am safe in saying that there are literally many hundreds of boards and' officers in Canada to-day authorized to exercise arbitrary power in dealing with the liberty and property of our citizens, and that free from any right of our courts to review such decisions.	.
Many of these boards are' not bound by their previous decisions; are free to put their own construction on the common law and the statute law; to revive the star chamber method if conducting their proceedings behind closed doors, and to give no reasons for their _ decisions; the wronged suitor being left without redress.	_	.
This legislative invasion of the people s rights is continuing with ever-increasing momentum, and will undoubtedly continue until an aroused public opinion teaches the people's representatives that the spirit of John Hampden still lives and demands the restoration of the people's rights, and regards every representative who fails to resist arbitrary legislation as an enemy and a traitor to Canada.
That is not the comment of someone participating in a debate in a partisan way or from partisan motives, it is the deliberate and carefully expressed statement of a dis-

tinguished and revered chief justice of our country.	I submit that its admonition
applies immediately to what is being attempted in the section which we have before us at the present time. The section as originally drafted left the issuing and cancellation of licences exclusively with the board. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) evidently has recognized that that was indefensible, and has sought to bring the matter within the control of the governor in council. May I point out to him that the governor in council conducts his operations behind closed doors, that the governor in council may be just as arbitrary as any other tribunal and not infrequently is most arbitrary. When, as regards imports and exports, it is left to the governor in council to say who is to be licensed and who is not to be licensed, without this parliament having indicated in advance the limits within which the governor in council shall act in a matter of that kind, it is a very distinct invasion of the fundamental rights of the people. When that invasion affects the rights of producers and consumers it is invading pretty well the rights of all classes in the country. It is to this aspect of the section that I wish to take the strongest exception.
With respect to exceptional occurrences which may arise and to which reference was made a few days ago by the minister, I can see every reason why a statute might be so framed as to make provision that in certain exceptional circumstances and to meet certain needs, of which parliament would be informed immediately, the governor in council might have authority to take action of an exceptional nature. That is all right, but this is not for action of an exceptional nature, it is conferring a general power on the governor in council to be exercised at any and all times, and that I think is entirely wrong.
May I make mention of another circumstance which I believe to be vital. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said at different times that the British government take certain rights and have certain powers and authority given to them. They argue that we ought to follow that example and that our government should have similar rights. I would take no exception to that as respects the present bill if the measure contained, as does the British legislation, all kinds of safeguards against arbitraiy action framed in the interest of consumers as well as producers. We would then have a very different measure from that which we have here. The point, however, which I wish to bring out at the moment

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
is this: The British parliament is in session practically the year round and the statutes in Great Britain require that as soon as any action is taken under any of these measures, it is to be reported immediately to parliament, or if parliament be adjourned as soon after its reassembling as possible. All action taken by the British government and by local boards under its legislation must be reported to both houses of parliament. With what result? You have parliament practically continually exercising the fullest supervision over any orders in council which may be passed by the King in council, and over regulations by any minister of a department. Here in Canada the time during which parliament is in session is much shorter, and it is during the period when parliament is not in session that we may expect the governor in council to be passing the various orders to which strong exception is likely to be taken. For these reasons I feel that this section should not be permitted to pass. I believe, if enacted, it will work unexpected hardship in a multitude of directions. In saying that, I repeat once more that if the government need exceptional power for exceptional purposes a section could be drafted and passed by this parliament which would give to them all that is required to meet any emergent situation.

His imagination, and particularly his suspicion, has lost nothing as a result of his rest over the weekend. I made it as clear as I could make anything, with my limited knowledge of English, that in the preparation of this bill there was no intention of putting it to the use which the right hon. gentleman suggested would be made of it in connection with empire trade-the use *which he said was the chief principle of the bill. To-day he repeats that he still believes it is intended to use the act based upon this bill to restrict trade with foreign countries for the purpose of increasing trade, or of directing the channels of trade, throughout the empire; and he also states that an endeavour is being made seeking to limit production.

I cannot understand why the right hon. gentleman, from the time the bill was introduced until the present moment, has persisted in reading into it, as one of its chief principles, the limiting of production, unless the reason is that having read that principle into the bill the first time it appeared before the house he feels it incumbent upon him to substantiate that assertion, repeated at least fifteen times in his original speech, with respect to what he considers to be the purpose of this legislation.
Let me repeat briefly now whait I have stated before, and let me try to make it if anything clearer on this occasion. No government in any country would pass legislation to restrict the export of primary products or of any of its commodities to any other country of its own volition; but we must remember that other countries are imposing quotas against imports into their territory. For example, Great .Britain might at the beginning of the year limit the exports of our cattle to the United Kingdom to 20,000 head for the year, let us say for the sake of illustration. Now, we have no say in that regard. But if the British parliament did pass such legislation it would be necessary for this government to have certain powers over exports to regulate the flow of that commodity out of this country into the United Kingdom; otherwise there would be a tendency on the part of those whose business it was to export cattle or to raise cattle for export to throw as many as they could on the old country market, and to do so immediately. And the old country would accept them until the quota had been filled. Then there would be an unnecessary glut of the market in Canada. And the throwing upon the British market at one particular time, and in a short space of time, of that number of cattle which we were allowed in our quota would be disadvantageous to our producers.
We do not know in that connection what action may be taken by any country to set up quotas, because I am told there are restrictions in trade, through the instrumentality of quotas, in more than twenty different countries, practically all European. France perhaps has come out more decidedly than any other country in the use of quotas as such to control trade, using them as an instrument of negotiation with other countries.
Here I should like to remind the leader of the opposition of something which apparently he has lost sight of completely. I believe that one of the greatest obstacles in Canada to the negotiation of trade with other countries is the most favoured nation treaty

introduced and put into practice by the government which the right hon. gentleman himself led; because as soon as any country offers to negotiate, or as soon as we approach another country with offers of negotiation, we find that we are tied to so many other countries that we are obliged to make similar arrangements with them. I have therefore no hesitation in saying that one of the greatest obstacles to the widening of our trade the world over through negotiation is this very treaty for which the government led by the right hon. gentleman himself was responsible.
I see nothing to be gained by the reprinting of this bill before the third reading. We have spent enough time on it, and every member of the committee should know it almost by heart.

With respect to what the minister says as to the use to which this measure may be put, namely to meet in the way he has indicated a situation that may arise in Great Britain, I take no exception. I will admit that he may use the measure as a means of helping to meet certain situations as they may arise, and in the way he has suggested. But I would point out with deference that he himself may not always be the minister; and even if he is, he may find himself subject to cabinet policies much broader than those of his own department. Indeed, the very clause which he says will be used in one way is equally capable of being used in quite another. I shall

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
illustrate. I will take the very example suggested by the minister. The minister says, assume for example that there are certain restrictions on cattle going to the British market. These would naturally be annoying to our producers. He then said, we can prevent certain shippers shipping all kinds of cattle, we can have regard for this provision and see that only certain classes are shipped. But is it not also possible that the government, seeing what the British government has done, may begin to follow a policy quite other than that which the Prime Minister has just laid down, namely the policy of making tariffs fight for the producers; and when the British government begins to restrict importations from Canada, immediately retaliate or threaten retaliation by restricting what in the way of imports may come in from Great Britain to Canada? Under this clause, as I read it, the government have the power of beginning a species of economic warfare between different parts of the British Empire, to say nothing of between Canada and other parts of the world, a species of economic warfare which may be wholly ruinous to interimperial trade as well as to trade in general. I think that possibility is there, especially When the Prime Minister himself, has elsewhere declared that part of his policy is to make tariffs fight for us. You have there a very clear assertion that some power is needed which will enable the government here-it would not be parliament, it would be the governor in council probably when parliament is not in session at all-to stop altogether certain importations into this country. I think parliament ought not to permit the possibility of any such thing, but parliament cannot prevent that possibility unless now, while it has the opportunity, it refuses to enact a clause of this kind.
Before the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) goes out, apropos of this provision, which here Carries regulation to the extent of prohibiting imports altogether, may I ask the minister if he. will tell us what has caused him so completely to change his whole point of view with respect to the excessive paternal regulation of trade. I have in my hand a statement made by the minister himself, on June 8, 1926, over so small a question as that of grading eggs. The Minister of Justice at that time waxed very eloquent with respect to a bill brought in simply to regulate the grading of eggs. Let me read what he said:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the whole system is wrong. Surely we can continue the open market system.
Well, this is not the open market system, this is a proposal to let the governor in council close the markets, both import and export. However, let me go on:
If you are going to grade eggs, why not grade other produce? Why not grade butter, fruit, potatoes and other vegetables, that are bought on the market? Why compel the farmers to undergo this grading system only in regard to their eggs? I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is an imposition upon the farmers of this country, and more particularly it is an imposition on the wives of the farmers. No injustice has been done in the past under the old system. Both purchaser and vendor have been satisfied with the old' open market system, where the good old doctrine of "caveat emptor" *-let the buyer beware-prevailed. Under that system the purchaser got the eggs he bargained for, and the vendor was satisfied with the manner in which his eggs were sold. But these regulations are carrying this paternal idea in government to excess.
If that was true in regard simply to the grading of eggs how can the Minister of Justice to-day justify a paternal system which may possibly preclude altogether either importation or exportation of certain commodities?

speechtext: It does not mention the word production. Here again I wish to take exception to the government's method of proceeding. They have referred over and over again to the British marketing legislation and said, we are proceeding along lines similar to the British marketing legislation. But if one looks at the British legislation one finds that it refers from beginning to end to production. In Britain they face the question squarely and say, production may be limited. But this government has not the courage to say it is restriction of production, they say they are simply restricting importation and exportation and trade. I ask again if it is not a fact that you cannot restrict the sale of particular commodities, either the importation or exportation, without that inevitably acting upon and restricting production? That is the whole purpose, that is the whole purpose of licensing.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is not the right hon. gentleman in what he has already said ad^ vocating that we do adopt a policy of restricted production? Because he quotes the British act as providing for a restriction of production.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The British act speaks about production. If my hon. friend will safeguard this legislation with the safeguards the British have thrown around their legislation, then I would be prepared to give him my support. The British act, first of all, takes care to see that different departments of the government are involved in any restrictions that may be imposed. In the second place, as I have already pointed out, the British act deals solely with imports and not

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
with exports of any kind. In the third place the British act provides that all legislation under that measure, before it can be of any force or effect at all, must receive the approval of both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. This act does not require anything of the kind; as has been said over and over again, its whole purpose is to get away from the House of Commons and the Senate and to allow the governor in council to do as he pleases with respect to the power given him under this legislation.
Take a specific example; assume that for some reason the government thought there were too many potatoes being grown in Canada. All the government would have to do would be to pass an order in council setting forth that in their opinion the total quantity of potatoes should be so much, and that in order to produce potatoes licences would thereafter have to be obtained by all potato growers which licences would set forth how much by way of the production of potatoes they would thereafter be permitted. The minister cannot say that that power is not in this bill. He may say he does not intend to use it in that way, but so long as it is there it can be so used. What is true of potatoes is true of every other natural product, whether it be a product of agriculture, of the fisheries or of the forests. The minister states that this act is going to be used as a means of combating embargoes and prohibitions in other countries, I can see that it will not be very long before under the guise of regulating trade, it will be used as a first class instrument of economic warfare through the imposition of prohibitions, quotas and other restrictions against countries that may adopt a similar attitude towards Canada.
Before we go in for a policy of that kind, it should be clearly sanctioned by this parliament, that we should not at this time put the House of Commons in a position where it can be said later on that the house consented to the governor in council having a power of the kind. The policy of scarcity is the base offspring of those base policies of economic nationalism and economic imperialism which are rampant in different parts of the world, and which are now being adopted in our own country; policies which everyone denounces when he speaks of what is at the bottom of the world's ills to-day, but which, apparently, no parliament is seeking to throw off, or at all events combat in the open way in *which they should be combatted. We find one country destroying its coffee, another destroying some
of its live stock, a third destroying something else; we even find our own government entering into agreements-without the consent, the knowledge or the authority of this parliament -limiting the total amount of wheat that can be produced in the country or sold abroad.
That is the kind of thing I meajn when I speak of a policy of scarcity. It is not only individuals in this parliament who feel aroused and riled about it; those in other walks of life who are most concerned with the well being of our citizens are beginning to protest openly against this vicious policy which aims at scarcity of production rather than at plenty. When I spoke on the address I was taken to task by the Prime Minister because I made a reference to the prayer book of the Anglican church. What do we find the Very Rev. Dean Riley saying, in the cathedral in Hamilton, as to the policy of scarcity? Let me quote a dispatch I hold in my hand:
"It's a damned blasphemy and I use these words advisedly," stated Very Rev. C. E. Riley, B.A., D.D.. Dean of Niagara, in a trenchant attack on the present system of distribution before a large congregation at the 92nd annual service of St. George's society of Hamilton, at Christ's Church cathedral last night.
That appears in the account of the Hamilton Spectator of April 23, and the report goes on to quote the dean's very strong denunciation of what he refers to as this business of legislators trying to limit production when they ought to devote their efforts to seeing that production is more plentiful and that there is a better and wider distribution. Let me quote the following comment upon the dean's utterances which appeared in another Hamilton paper the Hamilton Herald of April 26. It is as follows:
The outburst of the Very Rev. Dean Riley on Sunday evening may have shocked his audience, but the shock was nothing to what the people of the dominion have felt who are directly concerned with the results of the policy he denounced.
That is not an opinion quoted in England; that is the opinion of the dean of a cathedral in Hamilton, speaking of policies as he sees them in Canada at the present time.
His position was a reasonable and logical one.' The Anglican church in its comprehensive litany and collects lea\res little in human affairs out of consideration.
The prayers for harvest bounty and for happy seedtime are thoughtful and natural expressions. We pray to God "that it may please Thee to give and preserve to our use the kindly fruits of the earth so that in due time we may enjoy them"; and again-"Increase the fruits of the earth by Thy heavenly benedictions; and grant that we, receiving Thy bountiful liberality, may use the same to Thy glory"; and again-"We give Thee humble

thanks for this Thy special bounty, beseeching Thee to continue Thy loving kindness unto us; that our land may yield us her fruits of increase, to Thy glory and our comfort."
Surely the dean was justified in using the strongest language about those who profess to honour God and then deliberately take away from His children the opportunity of enjoying the kindly fruits they have prayed for; and all merely because they are not wise enough to plan for plenty, and too ignorant of the methods of commerce to do anything but blockade the traffic of the world.
That is what hon. gentlemen opposite are doing by this legislation, blockading the traffic of the world. This bill seeks to give power to the governor in council to control imports and exports as he pleases. In this very city, within the last week, while this House of Commons was debating this very question, another prominent divine gave utterance to words very similar. He happened to belong to a different denomination; I refer to Reverend Robert D. Whyte, former minister of Knox church in this city. I have in my hand the report of an address which the Reverend Mr. Whyte gave on May 22. In it I find the following:
"It is utterly fallacious and the wildest kind of insanity for Brazilians to burn their coffee, for New Zealanders to drive their sheep into the sea and for governments to drive farmers to keep acres out of production.
You could not get a more pointed statement in opposition to legislation such as that before us at the moment.

It is to that sort of thing that the people all over the country are taking exception. I venture to say that until this year, we in this parliament never heard a minister of the

crown advocate a policy of limiting production. It has been slipped in and along, one stage at a time, and now we have reached the point where the government demand the right to do as they please with regard to the restriction of imports and exports. I say that power never should be given to any body other than parliament itself. I believe, moreover, it is a power to which the governor in council has no right. The constitution of the country gives this parliament the sole control of trade and commerce. It does not provide that a body subordinate to this parliament shall be placed in a position superior to it. The trouble with the whole of this legislation is that it takes a number of subordinate bodies, tiny little local boards to begin with, then provincial boards and the board to be created by the governor in council, and finally the governor in council himself, and confers on all these subordinate bodies powers of legislation which are superior to those retained by parliament for itself. That is all wrong. That is contrary altogether to the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law, and should not be countenanced for one moment.

Before this section is disposed of I would like to submit that the criticism raised by the leader of the opposition has no particular reference to the bill itself but is a valid criticism of our general ignoring of the necessity of a new policy with respect to monetary matters. The criticism of artificial scarcity that the leader of the opposition raises is sound, and every act of this government and of his own government in the past was calculated rather to assist in the creating of scarcity, so that commercial and other eniteiprises might be able to profit by the higher prices that would ensue therefrom.
So far as this bill is concerned, my conception of it-I may be incorrect but I hope I am not-is that it purports to improve the marketing processes of the primary producer so that he will be able to secure a larger share of the consumer's dollar expended for the goods so marketed. If the bill has any other purpose I do not believe I would have supported it. As the leader of the opposition has said, under our present system and with your present type of ministers here and in other countries you cannot expect the introduction of a policy calculated to do what he implied ou^ht to be done, namely, to increase the purchasing power of the masses of the people. As long as you have your sound money system and your gold standard restrictions, as long as you have the present wholly unjust disparity in national income, just so long are you in the position of being compelled artificially to provide for scarcity, and the govern-
ment of the leader of -the opposition got no further away from that than the present government is getting away from it. We accept this bill only as a means of modifying slightly some of the inherent evils in a wrong monetary system. That is all. France presented the conference with a draft treaty for the definite limitation of production of a large number of basic commodities. The reference to Brazil has become almost classic in connection with monetary reforms. Six million bags of coffee destroyed last year and almost a million the year before. There was-a limitation of cotton in Egypt in 1926 and again in the state of Texas. We have this artificial restriction of production offered as a cure under the system under which we are now living. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) has just suggested to me that the leader of the opposition has not yet proposed a scheme by which there would be any increase of the volume of purchasing power on the part of the masses of the people in order to enable the consumption of the plenty which we are now undoubtedly capable of producing. In my opinion, that is the nub of the whole business. If hon. members will take the well placed words of the leader of the opposition and analyze them with respect to the general economic conditions and, general social system and work out a plan by which we shall endeavour definitely to consume production instead of trying to regulate, we would be on the fair road to happier days for all of us. The trouble with both Sir Basil Blackett and the leader of the opposition is that they have not related their broad conception of the trouble to the legislation necessary for monetary reform. We cannot lose sight of the fact that the masses of the people in this country 'have never yet received sufficient income to pay income tax. More than ninety seven and a half per cent of the Canadian people are below the income tax level of the dominion government. All the income tax that has ever been paid has been paid by two -and a half per .cent of the people. In the face of a scarcity of purchasing power of that kind, on the one hand, and a vast dominating wealth on the other, how is it possible to con-

tinue? The trouble with the present system is that there has never been a sufficient volume of purchasing power circulated by the present financial system. Never at any time. There are some free traders and mid-Victorian economists who protest that the mere act of production creates the necessary purchasing power, but that is not accepted to-day. Every modern economist states that there never has been and is not to-day a sufficient volume of purchasing power to take up consumption. Any student of modern finance knows that until we relate this problem to the point of view of consumption, even to more than consumption, it cannot be solved. speechtext: Before the clause carries I should like to draw the attention of the committee to what we are asked to do. We are being asked to fix penalties without knowing what the offences may be to which these penalties are to be attached. That is an entirely wrong position in which to place the House of Commons. Let me illustrate: Any local board, the existence of which is not yet known, the regulations of which will not be known until after it is formed, and the orders of which will not be known until after regulations are made, may give an order of a particular nature, and anyone who violates that order becomes liable to the fine and imprisonment for which we are now making provision. We are fixing the penalty to which some person or persons are to be subjected, although we have no idea what the offence itself is to be to which these penalties are to apply. That is wrong in principle. As I said a moment ago it is substituting local boards for parliament, and elevating these subordinate bodies into bodies having a power higher than that which parliament itself is prepared to exercise in the matter of the creation of offences. I do not believe that is a proper procedure or proper in any respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Of course this is the same argument, in principle, which the right hon. gentleman has mflde so many times in connection with this bill. Under many acts of parliament we give power to pass regulations about which we know nothing at the time the bill is passed, and we provide penalties for breaches of regulations. In this instance it is an order of a board; it is not a regulation, but the same principle is involved. We have done it; it is an established custom of parliament; no harm has resulted; no harm will result, and I cannot see any objection to it.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I suggest that what parliament has done, at the very most, has been to set out a class of offences and attached to those offences certain penalties. It has permitted the governor in council to make certain regulations under some general clause which applies from one end of the country to the other. But here we are permitting a condition whereby an act may be made an offence in one locality which may not be an offence in another. Under such a condition we make a person liable to fine and imprisonment in one part of Canada, while in another part of Canada at the same time there is no similar law, although parliament has fixed the penalty. I have quoted from the report of the Royal Commission on Ministers' Powers. There is one other passage I should like to quote in this connection. It is from page 72:
The best exposition of the modern doctrine-[DOT]
That is to say, of what the rule of law now means:
The best exposition of the modern doctrine and of its corollaries is that contained in Dicey's Law of the Constitution. He says: That "rule of law" which forms a fundamental principle of the constitution, has three meanings, or may be regarded from three different points of view. It means, in the first place, the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power, and excludes the existence of arbitrariness, or prerogative, or even of wide discretionary authority on the part of the government.
I submit that under that exposition what is here proposed is a highly improper method of proceeding, namely, to allow the governor in council arbitrary power to fix certain offences and to ask this parliament in advance of those offences being named or known, to fix the penalty that is to be made applicable when the governor in council has acted. The report goes on, still quoting from Dicey:
It means, again, equality before the law, or the equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law courts.
There again I submit that we are violating what is fundamental because under this legislation there will not be equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land. These penalties that we are now asked to enact will apply only here and there as different local bodies, the central board, or as the governor in council may wish to have them apply. The penalties are to be made applicable to offences that are created by these local boards. I believe it will be found such a procedure is wholly unconstitutional and I

Marketing Act
submit we ought not to be asked to enact legislation of the kind. Quoting again from the report, Dicey says finally:
The "rule law," lastly, may be used as a formula for expressing the fact that with us the law of the constitution, the rules which in foreign countries naturally form part of a constitutional code, are not the source but the consequence of the rights of individuals as defined and enforced' by the courts.
In other words, individuals have certain inalienable rights, one of which is not to have their property or person put in jeopardy for any offence that is not known, and which is not a part of the law of the land. But in this bill you are making a man liable to both fine and imprisonment, the extent of which is set forth in the enactment of this parliament for acts that to-day are wholly innocent and which will not become offences generally, and of which even the nature is not known at this very time the penalties which are to apply to them are being set forth.

I would point out further that the whole purpose of parliament is to see, when legislation is being enacted the effect of which is to deprive the individual of his personal liberty or his property, that at least it shall be enaated by those who have been elected to parliament under methods which are intended to ensure the representation of all classes. But this is the making of law not by representatives of

the people as a whole but by the representatives of occupational groups, and it may be a very limited group in a particular occupation, and is always a self-interested group. There are none of the safeguards here which the Dominion Elections Act affords to all classes whose rights and liberties are likely to be affected by legislation. [DOT] There is no secret ballot, no qualification of candidates, no qualification of voters-no parliamentary practice or procedure-none of the qualifications or obligation's required of those who are the recognized law makers. All these are thrown to one side, and hereafter any interested group for its own purposes, if it can get away with it, can make an offence to which the penalties now being framed by this House of Commons shall apply. Parliament itself under the constitution has exclusive powers in that regard. So far as giving the governor in council power to create the offences to which these penalties shall apply I submit that parliament is thereby simply handing over to the governor in council a function and a power which the constitution has reserved to parliament alone, and which parliament cannot properly divest itself of and give in its entirety even to the governor in council. The reason for this suggested amendment is that the by-laws of the company are not known to the public and under the recent decision in the Bank of the United States vs. Ross there is the suggestion that in every case in dealing with the company an outside party must insist upon the production of the by-laws in order that he may make himself acquainted with all the powers vested by the by-laws in an officer of the company. If the amendment is accepted it will then

read: "in general accordance with his powers either as expressed or implied." I think I had better allow the section to stand so that hon. gentlemen can see the effect of the amendment in the votes and proceedings to-morrow.

This is

On section 36-Invalid without entry.

It has been suggested that
after the word "transfers" in line 9 there should be inserted the words "or in a branch register of transfers." The fact is that many companies have a general register and also branch registers, and, in view of the decision in the Royal Bank vs. Smith case respecting provincial branch registers, it was really an oversight that these words were not inserted in the drafting.

Has consideration been given to the question of the registration of shares to make it obligatory on companies to open registers in the various provinces? I have in mind the question of succession duties and the payment of double fees. Nearly all the big corporations have their head offices in Montreal, Toronto or some other large city, while the shareholders are scattered throughout every province. There is no reciprocity between the provinces in the matter of succession duties, and very often the estates of deceased shareholders are mulcted for double duty. In the province of Quebec an incorporated company may claim a different province as its domicile, while the shareholder claims another province. This leads to a great deal of litigation and double expense. The banks have worked out a scheme for the relief of the estates of deceased shareholders. They provide a register in every province and it seems to me that this is the proper time and place to make it obligatory upon public companies to open share registers in every province. I have had a great deal of experience in connection with these matters and I know it works very great hardship, not on the companies but on the estates of deceased shareholders. I offer the suggestion that this clause be drafted in such a way as to provide that where there is any considerable number of shareholders in any one province, a company shall open a branch registry office in such province.

As a matter of fact, it is not obligatory upon the banks to open branch or provincial registers, but in provinces where there is a considerable number of shareholders
Dominion Companies Act

they do so for the personal convenience of their shareholders. Full provision is made in this bill for branch registers, but we have left it optional with the company as to the adoption of a branch registry system. This bill applies to every company incorporated, whether it be a small company with a thousand dollars capital or a large company with many millions of dollars of capital. After full consideration we thought that the time had not come to make the establishing of branch registers obligatory. In the case of the smaller companies it would be an obligation and burden which would be intolerable. I trust the hon. gentleman will allow this section to pass in its present form. I am ready to accept the opinion of the committee, but my own opinion is very dedidedly against making branch registers obligatory in a general statute which applies to all companies, whatever their capital may be.

I appreciate that in the case of the small joint stock companies it might be a burden, but I do suggest that in the case of companies whose shares are listed on the stock exchanges it should be made obligatory. I am quite satisfied the section could be drafted in such a way as to cover the cases I have in mind, that is, companies whose shares are listed on the stock exchanges. It should not be any great burden if this were done, and it would provide protection to the estates of deceased shareholders. This should be done for the very pertinent reasons which I have urged. Any hon. gentleman practising in the smaller provinces knows that in the case of a large estate with diversified investments and securities a great number of shares will be held in companies listed on the Montreal or Toronto stock exchanges. In the case of decedents residing in the smaller provinces there is a double taxation because the shares are registered in the province in which the head office is located. I understand there is a recent decision in Quebec which is under appeal and which would afford protection, but I think this is the time and place to give consideration to the circumstances which I have indicated, I am afraid very inadequately. If we do not do it now we will not get it done for many years to come. This bill is to be a model and I appeal to the minister to give some consideration to these suggestions.

I suggest that my hon. friend who has just spoken is approaching the matter from the wrong end. I submit that we are legislating for companies and not in connection with succession duties. I think there is a lot of room for improvement in the

succession duties acts and in the way they are administered, although I do not cast any reflection upon anyone. The double duty is caused not by the Dominion Companies Act but by the rulings which have been given by the various attorneys general and the various succession duties departments of the provinces. While I sympathize with my hon. friend, I submit he is approaching the question from the wrong angle. I have a case in mind of a small estate which is being virtually held up because of claims from two different succession duties jurisdictions. I suggest that it would be a serious thing for companies, even those listed on the stock exchanges, to be required to have registers in every province regardless of the fact that their shareholders may be residing in only two or three provinces.

I agree that we are legislating on behalf of all companies, but I suggest, with all deference, that we are also legislating on behalf of the shareholders of companies. I think that is a complete answer to the statement of my hon. friend.
They do not have to become shareholders.

In so far as their rights are affected by this bill, we are legislating just as much in the interests of shareholders as we are in the interests of the company. It would not be such a difficult thing to establish branch registers. The trust companies operate in every province, and all that would be required would be the appointment of a registrar in a particular province by resolution of the directors. It would necessitate the payment of a very small fee to affect the transfers I have in mind. I see no difficulty about it; in fact I am quite satisfied it could be worked out very easily and very economically. It would be of great benefit, not to the companies but to the shareholders, to whom they owe a duty in this respect.

Hon. gentlemen will remember that in 1932 I introduced a bill which created a new part to the Dominion Companies Act, a part which appears as part YI of this act, to be found at page 96. This part provides that all Canadian companies incorporated under any aot of the parliament of Canada or of the legislature of the late province of Canada may have branch registration offices. When introducing that legislation in 1932 we gave most careful consideration to the question raised by the hon. gentleman

Dominion Companies Act
with regard to branch registers. We provided by the terms of that enactment every facility for the opening of branch registers, with the result that many of the large companies have opened branch registers of their own volition in more than one province, but confining such branch registers to those provinces in which numbers of their shareholders were resident or domiciled. Shareholders have the option of not retaining shares in a company which fails to give them the protection which they think they ought to have in respect of the succession duties taxes. We have given the companies this option and have left it to the shareholders to bring pressure upon the company with respect to the establishing of branch registers. We think we have gone just about as far as we ought to go at the present time. This matter has been developed by a succession of decisions of the highest courts of the land, and I do not think we are yet in position to amend the Dominion Companies Act to provide for successful evasions of the decisions of provincial courts wth respect to the succession duties tax. I prefer to leave it as it is at the present time.

I must
take exception to the last statement of the minister. There is no attempt to evade the payment of any succession duties tax. I do suggest that we ought not to pass legislation which will help two different provinces to obtain succession duties on the same securities. That is what has happened in the past and it is what I have had in mind as an evil that ought to be cured if possible. I have heard no good answer yet as to why it should not be made obligatory. I have in mind the case of registered bonds of the Canadian National Railways. For years I had put up a battle with the treasury department of the Canadian National Railways to have their bonds registered, not in Montreal but in the place where the bondholder resides. I had a long correspondence with the late Mr. Ruel. I could not get him to move for a long time, but finally I did, so that the Canadian National Railway bonds might be registered in New Brunswick through a trust company, as they had previously been registered in Quebec. Take the expensive litigation in connection with the Sifton estate. If the Sifton bonds had not been registered in Montreal, where the head office of the Canadian National Railways was, the province of Quebec would have had no earthly excuse for trying to collect from the executors a huge sum of money in succession duties. We are perpetuating what is really a scandal in this country, namely, the collection of double duties on the same set of securities.
Are they collecting to-day two income taxes on the salaries of ministers who live in Ottawa? It is done every day, but does anyone suggest that that is a scandal?

I do not
know whether my hon. friend is defending the principle of double taxation in succession duties.

The idea of double taxation is not necessarily a scandal, which is the term my hon. friend uses. Anyone who has lived in Ottawa knows that the same income is taxed twice in the city of Ottawa-by the city and again by the income tax department. But no one uses strong language, calling it a scandal. The food we eat is taxed a good many times and no one talks about it as a scandal. I do not understand my hon. friend's argument. I appreciate the fact that there are hardships, but my point is that he is proposing to legislate in the wrong place. In the first place this is a companies act and we are not concerned with the question as to who shall or shall not purchase shares of a company, because after all that is a voluntary matter; and secondly, as the minister says, we are pretty nearly legislating to assist in an evasion of provincial law. How should we like it if the provinces started to legislate in the same way to assist in the evasion of a dominion law? We have to be careful about a matter of this kind, which is not as clear as my hon. friend suggests. Further, it is questionable whether we shall get clear of double taxation simply by making it obligatory upon companies to register in the different provinces. It is possible that there may still be double taxation, and my hon. friend may be enhancing the possibility not only of double but of treble taxation if that is done. As the Secretary of State has said, we are not yet at the stage, so far as judicial decisions are concerned, where we know precisely where we are in relation to the possibilities of succession duties in Canada and how far domicile enters into it. We do not know how far the question as to where you can effectively transfer property, which is the test in some instances, determines the liability for succession duty purposes. I know that my hon. friend has had far more experience than I in connection with succession duties, but I submit that we ought as far as
